C1: Yes. Blasphemy is a poison that defiles the whole commonwealth and draws God's wrath upon the realm, not merely on the offender. The magistrate bears the sword as God's minister and must cut it out. Nor should the penalty be weighed by earthly harm, for an insult to an infinite God is an infinite offense.

Yes. Our church and our crown stand together, and the faith of our fathers is what binds this nation into one people. Whoever mocks it publicly strikes at the common bond and gives comfort to foreign enemies who would divide us. Such speech is sedition in religious dress, and the law must treat it so.

No. Words that wound no one's body or property should never bring the whip or the gallows; the only real suffering in a blasphemy case is the prisoner's. If God is offended, He can answer for Himself. And a citizen's rights cannot depend on which creed he professes or rejects.

No. Laws exist to protect people, not ideas, and nothing is so sacred that it must be shielded from ridicule. Letting clerics decide what may be said about their doctrines hands them a veto over public life. A free society tolerates offense; it does not jail the heretic, the satirist, or the comedian.

In a limited form, yes. Deliberately insulting a minority's prophet or scripture is often a way of humiliating and endangering the believers themselves, and it can stir up mobs against them. Law should shield vulnerable communities from that kind of wounding abuse, just as it shields them from other targeted harassment, regardless of which faith is attacked.

Yes, but the penalty must fit the fault. A drunkard's idle oath deserves a small fine or an hour in the stocks; a deliberate, public reviling of Christ merits imprisonment. Burning men or boring their tongues for words is cruelty out of all measure, and it brings the law itself into contempt.

No. Forcing belief with fines and prisons defiles the conscience and fills the churches with hypocrites mouthing what they do not believe. Christ never gave the magistrate power over souls; the civil ruler keeps the peace, not the faith. Let error be fought with Scripture and prayer, never with the jailer's keys.

No. Blasphemy laws are really a tribe's way of policing its own dissenters and marking outsiders as enemies. Truth belongs to all humankind, not to one nation's altars, and a thinker in any land should be free to question the gods of his neighbors. Shielding a people's creed from challenge only breeds narrowness and suspicion.
C2: Yes. God commands children to honor father and mother, and the household is a little commonwealth in which the father rules as the king rules the realm. A child owes obedience not because the parent has earned it but because God placed him there; even a harsh father is to be obeyed.

Yes. A child is not a lone individual but a link in a family line, and the family's name and standing depend on its members holding together. Children who argue with their elders shame the household before the neighbors and weaken it against rivals. Obedience keeps the family united, and the family protects its own.

Yes. Every child is born with a willful, sinful nature, and if that will is not broken early it grows into pride, lust, and every corruption. Unquestioning obedience to godly parents is how the soul is kept clean and trained for heaven. A child left to follow its own desires is a child left to be defiled.

No. Teaching blind obedience leaves children defenseless against the adults who might hurt them, including, sometimes, their own parents. A child must know that they can refuse when something feels wrong and speak up without fear. Parents should guide and protect, but a rule of silent submission makes abuse easier to hide.

No. Children are persons with rights of their own, not their parents' property, and their views deserve a hearing in the decisions that shape their lives. Nor is a child's first duty to protect the family's reputation; a child who sees wrongdoing at home should be free to say so. Respect runs both ways.

No. A parent's claim to deference rests on the nurture, provision, and wise guidance they actually give; a father who neglects or abuses his children forfeits much of it. Children should obey while young and reason is weak, but the aim is to raise them into judges of their own conduct, not servants.

For the youngest children, largely yes. A three-year-old cannot weigh the danger of a busy road, a hot stove, or a stranger's car, and there is no time to explain when harm is seconds away. Prompt obedience keeps small children alive; explanations and debate can come as they grow old enough to understand.

No. The old notion that a child's will is tainted by sin and must be beaten out is a cruel superstition. Curiosity, questioning, and even defiance are healthy parts of growing up, not corruption. A generation drilled never to question its elders will grow up to obey any tyrant who takes the elders' place.
C3: No. A man's wealth is the fruit of his own labor, thrift, and risk, and he is entitled to keep what he has earned. Taking from the industrious to give to the idle punishes effort and rewards sloth. Differences in fortune reflect differences in diligence and talent, and flattening them is simply unjust.

No. Society is a great chain of ranks, each with its own duties: the lord to govern and protect, the laborer to work, the clergy to pray. This order was not invented by us and should not be torn up by us. Levelling estates by decree invites envy, faction, and ultimately chaos.

Yes. Every person shares the same basic dignity, and a society where a few own palaces while many cannot afford rent makes a mockery of that. Extreme gaps in wealth become gaps in political power, schooling, and health. Taxing great fortunes to fund common goods keeps citizens on something like the same footing.

Yes. Children go hungry, the sick go untreated, and the elderly freeze in winter while others live in abundance. That suffering is preventable, and the state is the only body large enough to relieve it reliably. There is no disgrace in accepting help when one is in need; the disgrace is in withholding it.

Yes. We are one nation, and a nation is a family on a larger scale. The prosperous owe something to their own countrymen, who fought the nation's wars and built its railways and factories. Sharing wealth among our people binds the classes together, keeps the nation strong, and leaves no divided, resentful populace for rivals to exploit.

No. Charity is a virtue only when freely given; money seized by the tax collector ennobles no one. Worse, a permanent state dole corrupts the poor themselves, breeding idleness, drink, and dependency, and degrading the self-respect that honest work instills. Relief belongs to churches, families, and neighbors who can guide the needy, not to government clerks.

Yes, and more than that. The wealth of the rich was produced by workers whose labor was paid a fraction of its worth; redistribution merely returns to them what they earned. And the claim is not bounded by flags: the miner in Bolivia and the weaver in Lancashire are robbed by the same owners.

No. Poverty is painful, but it is nature's spur to industry and prudence. Public relief only encourages the poor to marry early and multiply beyond what the land can feed, so that today's kindness becomes tomorrow's wider misery. The sympathetic impulse must yield to hard economic law; interference does more harm than good.
C4: Yes. My people share my language, my ancestors, my history, and my fate; they are my extended family. A man who claims to love all humanity alike usually loves no one in particular. Charity begins at home, and our first duty is to our own countrymen, before any stranger overseas.

No. A child starving in a distant country suffers exactly as much as a child starving down my street, and the accident of a border does not make her pain matter less. Where we can relieve great suffering cheaply abroad, patriotism is no excuse for looking away and spending lavishly on comforts at home.

No. Every human being has the same worth and the same rights, whatever passport they hold. Giving my own nation automatic priority is a kind of favoritism no different in principle from favoring my own race or class. Governments may serve their citizens, but morally, no one counts for more because of where they were born.

Yes, though rightly understood it is allegiance to one's sovereign. A subject is bound by oath and by nature to the prince God has set over him and to the laws of the realm. Talk of duties to all mankind is a dreamer's excuse for disobedience; the peace of nations rests on subjects keeping faith with their rulers.

No. My first allegiance belongs to God and to the community of believers scattered across every land. Nations and princes are passing things, and to exalt one's country above the divine law is a form of idolatry that stains the soul. Where my nation commands what God forbids, I must refuse it.

Yes. My nation schooled me, protected me, built the roads I travel, and sustains the institutions I rely on; its people have paid taxes and fought wars on my behalf. Obligations should track what we have received. Humanity at large, however worthy, has not given me that, so its claim on me is weaker.

Yes. Each people has its own soul, expressed in its tongue, songs, customs, and faith, and that inheritance must be kept whole and undiluted. Cosmopolitan fashions from abroad cheapen and corrupt it, reducing living cultures to a bland, rootless sameness. Guarding our own heritage comes first; humanity is enriched by distinct peoples, not by their dissolution.

No. Nations are banners that kings and generals wave to send poor men off to kill other poor men for someone else's profit. The worker in one land has more in common with the worker across the border than with his own rulers. I owe the flag nothing; I owe my fellow humans solidarity.
C5: Yes. Justice requires that the criminal receive what his deed deserves, measured by the gravity of the crime, not by any benefit to society. Even if a community were about to disband, it should first punish its last murderer. Letting a grave wrong go unanswered because punishment is 'useless' makes a mockery of the victim.

Yes. Innocent blood pollutes the land, and the stain remains until the guilty answer for it. A community that shelters a murderer from his due shares in his defilement and invites divine judgment on all. Punishment is not about usefulness; it is the cleansing of a wrong that otherwise lingers among us.

Yes. Even when a given sentence seems pointless, the majesty of the law depends on its being enforced without flinching. When judges soften sentences, the people learn that the crown's commands can be defied, and order begins to unravel. Severe, certain punishment proclaims that the law is sovereign and not to be trifled with.

No. Punishment is itself a harm, the deliberate infliction of suffering, and it can only be justified if it prevents greater suffering. Pain that deters no one, protects no one, and reforms no one is simply cruelty added to the world. Talk of what criminals 'deserve' is vengeance dressed up as justice.

No. Vengeance belongs to God, not to us, and Christ commands us to forgive as we have been forgiven. The worst sinner remains a soul capable of repentance, and the aim of any penalty should be his amendment. Heaping suffering on a man for its own sake hardens hearts, his and ours alike.

No. Harsh sentences never fall evenly: the poor, the foreign, and the despised fill the prisons and gallows, while the well-connected who commit grave crimes buy lenient terms or escape. A system that punishes severely for its own sake becomes an engine for crushing those at the bottom. Until justice is blind to rank, severity only deepens injustice.

Yes. When someone murders one of our own, the whole community is wounded, and we owe it to the victim and the grieving family to stand with them. Letting the killer off lightly because punishment is 'pointless' betrays our dead. Whoever turns on the community forfeits its protection and must face its full judgment.

No. There is no stain on society that a prisoner's suffering washes away; that is superstition. Severe punishment mostly serves the state's appetite for displaying its power. Better to focus on repairing harm: bringing offenders face to face with those they hurt, making restitution, and rebuilding lives, rather than caging people to satisfy officials.
C6: No. Marriage is a holy sacrament in which husband and wife become one flesh, and what God has joined no man may put asunder. Separation from bed and board may be allowed for grave cause, but the bond itself endures until death. To remarry while one's spouse lives is adultery and defiles the soul.

Rarely, if ever. The family is the foundation of the social order, with the husband at its head, and loosening the marriage bond loosens every other bond. A wife must bear patiently with her husband's faults, though he may put away an adulterous wife. Easy divorce would unsettle every household and leave society adrift.

Yes. No one should be trapped for life with a spouse who beats, terrorizes, or torments them, and children suffer when they grow up amid constant cruelty and fear. Forcing people to remain in such homes causes enormous, needless misery. Divorce is sometimes the only way to protect the vulnerable from ongoing harm.

Yes, and on the same terms for wives as for husbands. For centuries a man could cast off an unfaithful wife while she had to endure his infidelities and had no escape. Whatever grounds justify ending a marriage, they must be available to both partners alike, with property and custody divided without favoring either sex.

Yes, but only for grave fault such as adultery or willful desertion. The spouse who breaks the covenant has forfeited their claim on it, and the innocent party should be free to remarry. It would be unjust to chain a faithful wife or husband forever to one who has betrayed them, while the offender pays nothing.

No. When you marry, you pledge to stand by your spouse in sickness and poverty, through bad years as well as good. Walking away when things become hard is a betrayal of the person who trusted you and of the two families your union joined. Real commitment means staying, especially when it is difficult.

Yes, freely. Marriage is a private agreement between two adults, not a sacred mystery for priests or legislators to police. If both, or even one, no longer wish to continue, neither church nor state has any business binding them together. Nobody owes lifelong devotion to a promise made years ago by a different self.

Only in extreme cases. Whatever the parents feel, children are the ones who pay for divorce, shuttled between homes, torn between mother and father, and often poorer and more anxious for years. Adults who chose to have children should put their own unhappiness second and keep the home together unless there is real danger.
